Chapters

Wine glossary

The words of wine, explained in one line, with the chapter where they come from.

The vine

5 min read

Vines have been grown for centuries, above all in Europe: today about 60% of the world's vineyards are here. Italy and France are among the biggest producers, but in recent decades they have chosen to make less wine, of higher quality. Meanwhile new wine countries have grown (the United States, Chile, Argentina, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand).

In Italy wine is made in every region; the most productive are Veneto, Emilia-Romagna, Puglia, Sicily, Piedmont, Tuscany and Abruzzo. Next to the big numbers there are many small areas with their own character, often on slopes that are hard to farm.

The choices made in the vineyard (which variety, how to grow it, when to pick) decide most of a wine's quality. But every harvest is a story of its own: sun, rain, wind and frost change the result every year. That is part of what makes wine fascinating.

Vitis vinifera

The wine vine is called Vitis vinifera ("European vine", even though it was born in Asia). The first cultivated vines reached Italy about 4,000 years ago; the Etruscans let them climb up trees.

In the 19th century two scourges from America changed the history of European wine:

  • powdery mildew (oidium), a fungus that destroyed most French vineyards;
  • phylloxera, a tiny insect that attacks the roots and destroyed about 85% of European vineyards.

The solution was grafting: the European vine is "attached" to the roots of an American vine, which resist phylloxera. It is still done this way today. Many ancient varieties, however, were lost forever.

Planting a vineyard

The vine is a climbing plant with deep roots (in dry soil they can go down 5–6 meters looking for water).

New vines are not grown from seed, because the plants would differ from the mother. Two techniques are used:

  • cutting: a piece of branch planted in the ground grows roots. It gives "own-rooted" vines, of excellent quality but exposed to phylloxera;
  • grafting: a piece of European vine is joined to a resistant American rootstock (the part with the roots). It is the most used method.

Italy is a big producer and exporter of young vine plants.

The vine's life cycle

Over the plant's life

  • 0–3 years: the vine grows but gives no grapes.
  • 3–5 years: production increases.
  • 5–25 years: full maturity, the most quantity and quality.
  • After 25–40 years: old age, few grapes.

Old vines give few bunches but of great quality: in France you find vieilles vignes on the label (vines over 40 years old). Some varieties produce a lot and regularly (trebbiano, montepulciano, merlot), others less and more irregularly (nebbiolo, cabernet sauvignon, picolit).

Over one year

  • March: the soil warms up and the sap rises; drops come out of the pruning cuts (the "weeping of the vine").
  • April: buds open, leaves and shoots are born. A sudden frost at this moment can do a lot of damage.
  • May–June: flowering and fertilization. Cold and wind can disturb it; then some berries stay small and green.
  • Summer: the fertilized flowers become berries, still green and hard.
  • July–August, veraison: the berries change color (yellow or blue-violet) and ripening begins.
  • Mid-August to late October: harvest. Early varieties ripen first (pinot noir, pinot grigio, chardonnay); late ones after (barbera, nebbiolo, cabernet sauvignon, nero d'Avola).
  • Autumn–winter: the branches turn woody, the leaves fall and the plant rests until spring.

How grapes ripen

As it ripens, the berry grows, takes on color and the pulp becomes soft and sweet. At the same time acidity drops: underripe grapes, or grapes grown in cold areas, are more sour.

Natural yeasts live on the skins: if a berry breaks, the juice can start fermenting on its own and pick up unpleasant smells, like vinegar.

To decide when to harvest, growers look at three "ripenesses":

  • sugars and acidity: the balance between sweet and sour in the pulp. In hot areas they pick a little earlier so as not to lose freshness;
  • color and tannins (the substances in skins and seeds): the longer the grapes stay on the vine, the more structured and tannic the wine, but with a little less color;
  • aromas: the grape's aromas grow with ripening and then, if you wait too long, fade. In some varieties, like moscato, you can taste them just by eating a berry.

Ideally the three ripenesses arrive together: a sign that the variety is in the right place and the vintage was good.

Vine problems

The vine is delicate. It suffers from cold, spring frosts, hail, drought and too much rain. Over-fertilizing hurts too: the plant grows a lot but the grapes lose quality. For quality wines mostly natural fertilizers are used (manure, plant-based fertilizers).

The main enemies:

  • fungi: downy mildew (loves humid weather), powdery mildew (loves sultry heat), esca. A special case is Botrytis cinerea, a mold that usually ruins the grapes but in special conditions makes great sweet wines possible;
  • insects: mites, moths and leafhoppers. One leafhopper in particular spreads flavescence dorée, a disease that can kill the plant;
  • root parasites: phylloxera and tiny soil worms that spread viruses.

Integrated, organic and biodynamic

  • Conventional: fungicides and insecticides are used. They work, but they pollute, cost money, and over time pests become resistant.
  • Integrated pest management: few products, only when needed, and "good" insects are used to keep harmful ones in check.
  • Organic: no weedkillers or synthetic chemicals. Only natural remedies such as copper and sulfur are allowed.
  • Biodynamic: born from the ideas of the philosopher Rudolf Steiner (early 1900s). It aims at the balance of the soil and the rhythms of nature, uses plant preparations to strengthen the vines, respects useful insects and grows vines only in the best-suited places.

The vineyard

6 min read

A vineyard is a small ecosystem: variety, soil, climate and human work must get along to give grapes rich in color, sugars and aromas.

There are two big philosophies:

  • the place first (typical of France and Italy). The French call it terroir: not just the soil, but climate, exposure, microclimate and tradition together. A cru is a small, precise area with unique features. In Italy this idea lives in the denominations of origin (DOC, DOCG);
  • the grape first (typical of "new world" countries: California, Chile, Argentina, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand), where wine is presented mainly by the name of the grape.

The truth is in the middle: a great wine comes from the right meeting of variety and place.

Variety and rootstock

Not every variety adapts everywhere:

  • some do well almost anywhere, like chardonnay, merlot and cabernet sauvignon;
  • others are demanding, like pinot noir and above all nebbiolo, which gives its best almost only in Piedmont (Langhe) and Valtellina.

The risk is chasing the "safe" varieties and abandoning local ones: Italy has a huge heritage of varieties to protect.

Within each variety there are many clones, "versions" with slightly different features (bunch size, color, sugars, aromas). Sangiovese, for example, has more than 100.

Native and international

  • Native: a variety born in an area and grown there for a very long time. Examples: nebbiolo, albana, schiava, grignolino, fiano, brachetto, croatina.
  • International: a variety now grown all over the world, almost always with excellent results. Examples: chardonnay, sauvignon blanc, riesling, cabernet sauvignon and franc, merlot, pinot noir, syrah.

In a few areas (for example Valdadige, Chile and Portugal) vines still grow without American rootstock, because phylloxera can't spread there.

Latitude and altitude

The vine likes neither cold nor excessive heat. It grows best in a precise band of the planet: in our hemisphere between the 40th and 50th parallel (Italy is in the middle of this band), in the southern one between the 30th and 40th. Exceptions are areas further north like the Mosel and the Rhine in Germany, famous for very aromatic riesling and gewürztraminer.

In Italy about 60% of vineyards are on hills, 32% on plains and 8% in mountains. The best wines come mostly from hills and mountains. Some areas, like Valtellina, Valle d'Aosta and the Cinque Terre, are so steep that people speak of heroic viticulture: almost everything is done by hand.

The higher you go, the cooler the air: in the south the best grapes often come from hills up to 600 meters; in the north vines do well lower down too; in Alto Adige and Valle d'Aosta they reach 800–1,200 meters.

Nearby water (rivers, lakes, sea) helps: it keeps the right humidity and at night gives back the heat stored during the day, avoiding sharp swings.

Zoning: studying an area to understand which vineyards are the best. In Barolo, for example, historic vineyards such as Cannubi, Cerequio, Bussia and Vigna Rionda have been recognized.

Why hills and mountains help

  • more sun on the leaves, so more sugars;
  • cool nights and hot days: more acidity and more elegant aromas;
  • more wind, so less mold;
  • less water in summer: the plant puts its energy into the grapes.

The soil

The vine doesn't want fertile soil: it prefers poor soil. The type of soil leaves a mark on the wine:

  • limestone and marl (limestone and clay): colorful, aromatic, structured, long-lived wines;
  • limestone with sand: balanced, fine wines, not always made for long aging;
  • clay: ideal for red grapes; colorful, complex, soft, long-lived wines;
  • sand: lighter, fresh, fragrant wines to drink young;
  • acidic: light-colored, fresh wines with little alcohol and structure.

Some famous examples: the slate of the Mosel and the gneiss of Alsace give white wines with "mineral" notes; the gravel of the Médoc holds heat and gives it back to the bunches at night; the red earth of Coonawarra (Australia) gives reds with notes of mint.

Texture matters too: sand makes soil light and well-drained, clay holds water and nutrients (but too much suffocates the roots), silt is in between. The best soils have a balanced mix of the three.

Climate

Climate changes every vintage. Nets are used against hail and sometimes irrigation against drought, but there's only so much people can do.

The vine wants mild temperatures (the ideal by day is around 25–28 °C). Even more than temperature, what matters is the day-night temperature swing, the difference between daytime heat and night-time cool: it gives more intense, elegant aromas and good acidity. A cool wind keeps molds away. Rain is useful in spring and summer, but close to harvest it's a problem: it "washes" the skins and the wine comes out less colored and less aromatic.

The microclimate is all these conditions together in a small area: it's what gives each vineyard its character.

Work in the vineyard

Human work in the vineyard can improve quality a lot: it's one of the reasons wine has improved so much in recent years.

Planting density. Today vines tend to be planted closer together. Each plant gives fewer bunches, with smaller berries: proportionally there's more skin, so more color and more aroma. More than the quantity per hectare, what matters is how many grapes each plant makes.

The orientation of the rows matters too: in the north growers look for more sun, in the center-south they try to avoid the strongest midday sun.

Thanks to sunlight, the leaves turn water and air into sugars (photosynthesis), which then end up in the berries and make them sweet. That's why leaves need good exposure.

Training systems

It's the "shape" given to the plant. It must expose the leaves well to the sun and let air move between the bunches.

  • Tendone and very tall shapes: lots of grapes, but less elegant wines with "green" notes. Little used today for quality.
  • Bush vine (alberello): an ancient, low shape of Greek origin, with no supports, perfect in the hot climates of the south (and on Pantelleria).
  • Pergola (Trentino-Alto Adige): the leaves shade the bunches.
  • Vertical trellis (Guyot, spurred cordon): the most common shape today. Vines grow in rows along wires, with the leaves vertical. It gives the best quality. In Europe Guyot dominates, in the rest of the world the spurred cordon, simpler to manage and suited to machines.

Pruning

It decides how many grapes the plant will make and gives it shape.

  • Winter pruning: choosing how many buds to leave. Few buds mean fewer but better grapes; many buds, more quantity.
  • Green pruning (spring–summer): useless shoots and extra leaves are removed so the bunches get light and air.
  • Green harvest (from late July): some bunches are cut and dropped to the ground, so the ones left become more concentrated and flavorful.

The soil is also worked, to aerate it and remove weeds. In very dry climates (Australia, Spain, Chile, Argentina) drip irrigation is used. In Italy many denomination rules forbid it.

The harvest

  • By hand: the gentlest. Only the best bunches are chosen and carried to the winery in small crates, without crushing them. If the berries break, the juice starts fermenting or oxidizing too early and the wine loses aromas.
  • By machine: fast and convenient, widely used abroad, but hard on Italy's steep vineyards.

In very hot areas grapes are even picked at night, in the cool, to protect them.

When to pick depends on the wine you want to make:

  • early: more acidity and fresh aromas, ideal for sparkling and fresh wines;
  • later: more sugar, so more alcoholic, structured wines;
  • much later (late harvest): overripe grapes for sweet wines, sometimes with "noble rot";
  • in midwinter, with frozen bunches: ice wines (Eiswein or Icewine).

The grape

3 min read

There are thousands of wine grape varieties in the world, but about fifty cover almost all vineyards. Some do well everywhere (chardonnay, cabernet, merlot), others give their best only in their own area: nebbiolo in Piedmont, teroldego in Trentino, picolit and pignolo in Friuli, glera in Veneto, lambrusco in Emilia, verdicchio in the Marche, sagrantino in Umbria, fiano in Campania, aglianico in Campania and Basilicata, nero d'Avola in Sicily.

Soil, climate and cellar work matter, but the grape gives the wine its imprint. A nebbiolo or a pinot noir will never have the dark color of a syrah or a nero d'Avola. A moscato or a sauvignon will always have a far more recognizable scent than a trebbiano.

The bunch

The bunch is made of berries attached to a small branch called the stalk. It can be tight or loose, small or large, cylindrical, conical or "winged".

The stalk contains hard, bitter tannins. That's why in the winery it is almost always removed (destemming), even for red wines.

The berry

The berry has three parts, and each gives the wine something different:

  • seeds: they contain aggressive tannins, which is why they must not be crushed;
  • pulp: the biggest part, with water, sugars and acids. In the center, near the seeds, it's more acidic; in the middle zone it's sweeter;
  • skin: just a small part of the weight, but it holds color, tannins and aromas. It may be the most important part.

On the skin there is often a white film, the bloom, which protects the berry and holds the natural yeasts. These yeasts can start fermentation on their own, sometimes with faults (a vinegar smell): that's why grapes must be processed right after picking.

The skin: color, tannins and aromas

Color

  • In red grapes, color comes from pigments called anthocyanins, which give young red wines their purple and ruby. Each variety has a different "mix", which is why color helps recognize wines: nebbiolo gives a lighter, orange-tinged red, barbera a very deep red.
  • White grapes have other, yellow pigments.
  • In some rare grapes (called teinturiers, like ancellotta) the pulp is red too.

Tannins

They're the substances that make your mouth feel dry (astringency, like biting an unripe persimmon). They give body and structure to reds. When young they are "rough"; with time they soften, and the color of reds moves from ruby to garnet and orange.

The riper the grapes, the more tannins and a little less color. That's why for reds it's important to decide how long the juice stays in contact with the skins.

Color and tannins also protect wine from air. It's one of the reasons whites, which have very few, are more delicate and oxidize more easily. The skin also contains resveratrol, a substance studied for its possible benefits for the heart.

Aromas

The skin is full of scented substances. In a few varieties, like the moscatos, you can smell the aromas just by eating a berry: these are aromatic varieties. In the others the aromas are "hidden" and released during fermentation and aging.

Some typical aromas:

  • herbaceous notes, of green pepper and tomato leaf: cabernet, merlot and above all sauvignon;
  • petrol notes (kerosene): some Rieslings aged in bottle;
  • vanilla and spicy notes: chardonnay, which is why it marries well with wood;
  • in general fruity, floral, mineral, vegetal and spicy aromas (pepper, cloves, licorice, rose).

The place changes mostly the intensity of the aromas, much less their character: a nebbiolo stays recognizable wherever it grows. There are exceptions, like sauvignon from the Loire Valley, where the soil really makes the difference.

The wine

12 min read

Wine is not a drink like the others: its history has always been entwined with ours.

A short history

  • The origins: it was probably born by accident, from forgotten grape juice that fermented. It was already made along the Tigris, the Euphrates and the Nile, often with added spices and honey.
  • Greeks: wine becomes the drink of rites and feasts. From Greece the vine spreads around the Mediterranean and reaches Sicily around 500 BC (the bush vine is a Greek legacy). In Italy, though, the Etruscans were already there.
  • Romans: they studied vines and wine in depth, kept it in amphorae and took it all over Europe. They loved aged wines, like the famous Falernian.
  • Middle Ages: monks (Benedictines and Cistercians) saved and improved viticulture.
  • Renaissance: vineyards spread enormously and people drank a lot, up to 200 liters a head per year.
  • 1600–1700: the glass bottle and the cork arrive, and the first sparkling wines refermented in bottle are born. In 1716 Cosimo III de' Medici marked the boundaries of Chianti, Pomino and Carmignano: the ancestor of today's denominations of origin. Soon after, Marsala is born.
  • 1800s: powdery mildew and phylloxera devastate European vineyards. Louis Pasteur discovers how yeasts work: modern enology is born.

What wine is made of (in short)

Wine contains hundreds of substances, but a few groups are enough to understand it:

  • water: the main part;
  • alcohol: it comes from fermenting the sugars; it gives warmth and softness;
  • acids: they give freshness and make you salivate, and you feel them most in young wines. The "good" acids are felt in the mouth; acetic acid (the one in vinegar) is felt on the nose and is a fault;
  • polyphenols: color, tannins and part of the aromas;
  • minerals: they contribute to savoriness (the "salty" feeling);
  • aromas: the scents.

The character of some varieties

Each variety has its own profile, easiest to taste in wines made from a single grape (single-varietal):

  • cabernet franc: blackberry, blackcurrant, violet, pepper;
  • merlot: black fruit (cherry, plum), more body;
  • sangiovese: berries (blackberry, blueberry), pepper and spice;
  • montepulciano: deep ruby color, ripe fruit, jam, bitter almond, firm tannins;
  • nebbiolo: very long-lived wines;
  • moscatos (white, pink, from Pantelleria…): very aromatic, with notes of citrus and flowers, ideal for sweet and sparkling wines.

Red, white and rosé: the difference

It all depends on how long the juice stays with the skins, because the color is in the skin:

  • red: the juice ferments with the skins and takes their color and tannins;
  • white: the skins are removed right away. You can make a white wine from red grapes too;
  • rosé: the contact with the skins is short.

With time a red moves from ruby to garnet and orange. A white, if it gets too much air, can turn yellow and darken.

From grape to must

The harvest date is decided by tasting the grapes and analyzing sugars, acidity, color and aromas. In Italy grapes are still often picked by hand, choosing the best bunches in the vineyard; in the winery there's often another selection on sorting belts.

Then the grapes become must, the juice:

  • for reds: the stalks are removed and the berries gently crushed (crushing);
  • for whites: whole bunches are pressed gently to get a clean juice (the free-run must) without extracting bitter substances from skins and stalks.

What's left (skins and seeds, the pomace) goes to the distillery and becomes grappa.

The must

Must is mostly water (70–80%) and sugars (about 18–25%), then acids, color, aromas, minerals and vitamins.

  • The more sugar in the must, the more alcohol in the wine. With overripe or dried grapes the sugar rises a lot.
  • To make a sweet wine, fermentation is stopped before all the sugar turns into alcohol.
  • Acidity makes wine fresh and pleasant; acetic acid (vinegar) must stay very low.

Yeasts, bacteria and molds

  • Yeasts: the stars. They turn sugar into alcohol. The most important is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same one used for bread and beer. Today selected yeasts are often used, chosen to bring out aromas or for sparkling wines.
  • Bacteria: usually harmful, but some are useful because they carry out malolactic fermentation, which softens the wine.
  • Molds: they usually ruin the grapes. The one exception is Botrytis cinerea, which in certain conditions becomes noble rot and makes the great sweet "botrytized" wines possible.

Sulfites and adjusting the must

Sulfur dioxide (the sulfites you read on the label) is the most used help in the winery: it protects must and wine from oxidation and stops unwanted microorganisms.

Sometimes the must needs adjusting:

  • if it has too little sugar (cold vintages): in Italy adding table sugar is forbidden (in some colder European countries it's allowed). Instead, concentrated must, grape sugar, is added;
  • if it has too little acidity: tartaric acid (the grape's natural acid) is added;
  • there are also modern techniques that concentrate the must by removing some water.

Making red wine

From the same grape, for example pinot noir, you can make a red, a rosé, a white or the base for a sparkling wine. Only the time in contact with the skins changes.

The main steps:

  1. Gentle destemming and crushing.
  2. Fermentation with maceration: the must ferments with the skins in big tanks (today almost always steel). In the first days mostly color comes out, then tannins and structure. Maceration usually lasts 10–15 days: less for light reds to drink young, up to 4 weeks for great reds made to age.
  3. Temperature control: fermentation produces heat, and if it gets too hot the aromas are ruined and the yeasts die. That's why tanks are cooled. Reds ferment at around 25–30 °C.
  4. The cap: the skins rise to the top and form a compact layer. To mix them back in, the cap is broken or the must is pumped back over the skins (punching down and pumping over).
  5. Racking off the skins: when fermentation ends, the wine is separated from the skins, which are then pressed gently.
  6. Then come malolactic fermentation, maturation in steel or wood, rackings, stabilization, bottling and aging in bottle.

Carbonic maceration and Novello

Novello is inspired by French Beaujolais Nouveau. Whole bunches are left for a few days in tanks full of carbon dioxide: inside the berries a kind of fermentation begins that develops intense aromas. The result is a wine with bright color, fruity and floral aromas, fresh and with light tannins, to drink right away, not to age. It's the only wine that can be sold as early as November of the harvest year (from November 6); the vintage is mandatory on the label.

Rosé wines

The most common method is a short maceration with the skins. Lightly colored red grapes or a mix of white and red grapes can also be used. What you can't do is mix red wine and white wine.

Despite their color, rosés are closer to whites than to reds: delicate, fragrant, fresh, to drink young.

Making white wine

The skins are removed right away, with a soft pressing of whole bunches. Fermentation happens at lower temperatures (18–20 °C) to keep the delicate aromas.

For richer, longer-lived whites the juice can be left with the skins for a few hours, in the cold, so it takes on more aroma. With this technique pinot grigio can also give "copper" colored wines (onion skin).

Alcoholic fermentation

It's the heart of everything: yeasts turn sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide (the bubbles), plus many other substances that give aroma and flavor.

On the label alcohol is shown as % vol. On sweet wines you sometimes find two numbers, like 11 + 5%: the first is the alcohol already there, the second the alcohol you'd get if the remaining sugar fermented too.

Malolactic fermentation

In spring, some bacteria turn malic acid (sharp, like a green apple) into lactic acid (sweeter and gentler, as in milk). The wine becomes less acidic, softer and rounder, and often picks up aromas of butter, hazelnut and vanilla.

It's typical of reds, but today it's also done in some important whites, often aged in barrique (for example certain Chardonnays).

Maturing and aging

Before going into bottle, the wine rests:

  • only in steel, for a few months: it keeps its fruit, freshness and the character of the grape. This is the case of most whites, rosés and young reds, bottled the spring after harvest;
  • in wood, for one or more years: the wine becomes softer and more balanced and develops a more complex scent, the bouquet.

Wood lets through very little air: tannins soften, the wine becomes more elegant and takes on new aromas. The most used wood is oak; chestnut and cherry were once used too.

Casks and barriques

  • Large cask (up to 150 hectoliters): thick walls. The wine changes slowly and you barely taste the wood. It's the tradition of Italy's great reds.
  • Barrique (a small barrel of about 225 liters): thin walls and lots of wood in contact with little wine. The wine changes faster and takes more aroma from the wood.

What wood gives the wine

  • color: reds move from purple-ruby to garnet and orange; whites from straw yellow to golden and even amber;
  • aromas: vanilla, butter, spice, coconut, toast, coffee, cocoa, tobacco, leather, dried fruit, jam;
  • a new barrique is very noticeable; one used once or twice much less;
  • the inside of barrels is toasted over a fire: the more toasted, the more vanilla, coconut, spice and smoky notes come out.

Where the wood comes from matters too: French oaks (for example Allier, Tronçais, Nevers) give fine, elegant woods, suited to whites as well; Slavonian oak is the classic choice for large casks; American oak gives stronger notes, with hints of coconut.

The risk is that the wood covers the wine. On an important wine barrique improves things; on a simple wine it erases its character. That's why part of the wine often rests in steel and part in wood, and then they're blended.

Some wines rest on the lees (sur lie): they become richer and more protected, especially if the lees are stirred often (bâtonnage).

In the end the wine goes into bottle, where it can age even for decades. There, with almost no air, color, balance and aromas improve. It happens to great reds, but also to some whites like certain Chablis and Rieslings.

Cellar work before bottling

  • Racking: the wine is moved from one container to another to leave the deposits (the lees) at the bottom.
  • Topping up: barrels must always stay full, because air would spoil the wine.
  • Fining and filtering: they make the wine clear and stable. Some producers choose not to filter, so as not to take anything away from the wine; the label says "unfiltered", and a small deposit is normal, not a fault.
  • Governo all'uso toscano: a Tuscan tradition of adding a few dried grapes to the new wine to make it referment, becoming more colorful, aromatic and round.
  • Pasteurization: used only for ordinary wines; the wine becomes stable but loses aromas.
  • Before bottling a little sulfite is added to protect the wine. Sometimes, in a just-opened wine, you smell a light pungent note: give the wine a little air and it goes away.

Bottling

Wine is bottled avoiding air, sometimes using neutral gases like nitrogen.

  • The only container for quality wines is glass, which doesn't change the taste. Bag-in-box and plastic are fine only for simple wines to drink soon.
  • Closures:
    cork: the classic for fine wines and wines to age, because it lets the wine evolve. Its flaw is a possible "corked" taste;
    synthetic or silicone: for wines to drink soon, cheap and neutral;
    screw cap: widely used in Australia and New Zealand even for excellent wines, especially whites. It avoids cork taint completely and no longer means cheap wine;
    glass: elegant but rare.
  • Over the cork there's the capsule (plastic, tin or aluminium), sturdier on fine wines.

The bottle

A bit of history. For centuries wine was kept in amphorae, jars and skins. Until the 1700s it was sold loose, in barrels, and the innkeeper served it in a carafe. The first blown-glass bottles, short and round, were born in France in the early 1700s.

The color of the glass. Light spoils wine. That's why quality wines go into dark glass (green, brown, amber). Clear glass is used for wines to drink soon, to show their color (whites and rosés).

Sizes

  • quarter: 0.20 l
  • half bottle: 0.375 l (often for passiti)
  • standard bottle: 0.75 l
  • magnum: 1.5 l (2 bottles)
  • giant sizes, mostly for sparkling wine and Champagne: jeroboam (4 bottles), rehoboam (6), methuselah (8), salmanazar (12), balthazar (16), nebuchadnezzar (20).

Shapes (almost all born in France, each tied to an area):

  • Bordeaux: the most common, with high "shoulders". Born in Bordeaux; dark for reds, clear for whites;
  • Burgundy: no shoulders, a soft profile, for Burgundy wines and many others;
  • albeisa: a dark bottle from the Langhe for the great Piedmontese reds, used only by the producers of one consortium;
  • Rhine/Alsace: tall and slim; in Italy used for aromatic whites;
  • bocksbeutel (or pulcianella): round and flattened, typical of Franconia in Germany; the pulcianella is sometimes used for Orvieto;
  • Port: for fortified wines (Port, Madeira, Sherry);
  • amphora: a curvy shape, tied in Italy to Verdicchio (1950s).

The cork stopper

Cork is the bark of the cork oak, which grows in Portugal, Spain, Sardinia and Corsica. The bark is stripped every 9–10 years without cutting the tree down, then seasoned, boiled, cut and worked into stoppers.

Cork is light, elastic and waterproof, and it seals the bottle neck perfectly. It lets through tiny amounts of air, which let the wine evolve slowly: the color softens, the aromas grow more complex, the taste more mature.

"Corked" taste is an unpleasant smell of mold and wet cardboard. It's caused by a substance (TCA) that forms because of molds and bacteria in the cork. It ruins the wine and can't be removed.

Wine composition and tasting

2 min read

Wine contains hundreds of substances. Some come from the grape, others are born with fermentation, others still with aging in barrel and bottle. Together they decide how a wine looks, smells and tastes.

Color

It depends on the variety, how ripe the grapes were, how long the juice stayed with the skins, where the wine rested and its age.

  • Reds: young they are ruby or purple and bright; with the years they turn garnet and then orange.
  • Whites: young they are straw yellow; with time and wood they turn golden, up to amber in passiti and fortified wines.

Aroma

Aromas fall into three families:

  • primary: they come from the grape. Flowers, fresh fruit, herbs, vegetal and mineral notes. You smell them most in young wines;
  • secondary: born during fermentation. More fruity and floral notes, and the "vinous" scent of young reds, which recalls the must;
  • tertiary (the bouquet): born with aging in barrel and bottle. Spice, toast, leather, tobacco, dried fruit, jam.

Taste: softness and hardness

In the mouth, wine is a balance between two groups of sensations.

Softness (makes the wine round and enveloping)

  • sugars: in dry wines you don't taste them, but they help softness; in sweet wines they give sweetness;
  • alcohol: gives a feeling of warmth, light in a Moscato, very strong in an Amarone. It also makes the wine softer;
  • glycerol: a substance born with fermentation that gives softness and "richness" (it's abundant in noble-rot wines).

Hardness (gives structure and liveliness)

  • acidity: gives freshness and makes you salivate. It's higher in young wines and sparkling wines, and also makes the color brighter;
  • tannins: they make the mouth feel dry (astringency), sometimes with a slight bitterness. Young they're rough; after aging in wood they become softer and more elegant;
  • savoriness: the "salty" feeling given by minerals. It's very important above all in whites, which have no tannins.

A wine is balanced when softness and hardness offset each other.

Bubbles (carbon dioxide) tingle the tongue, lift the aromas and make acidity and savoriness more noticeable, sweetness and warmth less. Their stream in the glass is called perlage.

A tiny touch of "volatile" acidity (the vinegar kind) can add freshness; too much becomes a fault.

Wine faults

Today wineries are clean and high-tech, so problems are rare.

  • Alterations: changes in color or clarity due to air or too much iron. For example a white that darkens and smells "cooked" or of Madeira (oxidized or maderized), or a wine that turns cloudy.
  • Diseases: caused by bacteria, for example those that turn wine into vinegar. They hit mostly weak wines, with little alcohol and acidity.
  • Faults: unpleasant smells that come from outside, above all cork taint and the pungent smell of too many sulfites.

The Classic Method

4 min read

Bubbles can be made in several ways, but the finest come from refermentation in the bottle: the Classic Method, the same as Champagne.

A good Classic Method wine is between straw and golden in color, with aromas of yeast, fresh bread, bread crust, brioche, biscuits, white flowers, fresh or dried fruit, sometimes mineral notes. The taste is elegant and long. The bubbles are fine and keep rising in the glass.

The base wines

The ideal grapes are chardonnay, pinot noir and pinot blanc (in Champagne also pinot meunier). Bunches are picked by hand, without crushing them, and pressed within a few hours very gently, taking only the best juice.

The juice ferments slowly, in the cool, and becomes a still base wine (no bubbles). Often each vineyard and each grape is vinified separately, to have many different base wines to combine. Some is kept for the following years.

The steps, in short

  1. Blending (cuvée): the winemaker tastes the base wines and blends them to create the house style, the same every year. Wines from previous vintages can be added.
  2. Liqueur de tirage: a little sugar and yeast is added to the wine.
  3. Bottling: in thick, dark bottles closed with a crown cap (like a beer cap).
  4. Second fermentation: in the cellar, cool and dark, the yeasts eat the sugar and make a little alcohol and the bubbles, which stay trapped in the bottle. Inside, pressure reaches about 6 atmospheres, three times a car tire.
  5. Aging on the lees: the dead yeasts stay in the wine and slowly release substances that give the typical bread and brioche aromas and make the bubbles finer. The minimum is usually 18 months (24 for vintage wines), but great producers go to 3 years and more, up to 7–8.
  6. Riddling (remuage): the bottles are turned and tilted a little at a time until they stand upside down, so the yeast deposits slide toward the cap. It used to be done by hand on pupitres (wooden racks), today often by machine.
  7. Disgorging (dégorgement): the neck is frozen, the cap removed and the pressure shoots out the ice plug with the deposits. The wine stays clear without filtering. The disgorging date on the label helps you know how fresh the sparkling wine is.
  8. Dosage: a little liqueur d'expédition is added, a secret mix of wine and sugar that decides how dry or sweet the wine will be. If nothing is added it's pas dosé (zero dosage).
  9. Final corking: with the classic mushroom cork, the wire cage and the capsule (which many people collect).
  10. Packaging and label, then a few months' rest before sale.

Vintage, non-vintage, blanc de blancs

  • Vintage (millesimato): made with grapes from a single year (at least 85%), shown on the label. Usually finer and aged longer.
  • Non-vintage (sans année): wines from previous years are blended in too.
  • Blanc de blancs: white sparkling wine made only from white grapes (mostly chardonnay).
  • Blanc de noirs: white sparkling wine made only from red grapes (mostly pinot noir).

How sweet is it? (from driest to sweetest)

  • Pas dosé / Brut nature / Zero dosage: practically no sugar
  • Extra brut: very dry
  • Brut: dry, the most common
  • Extra dry: dry but a little softer
  • Sec / Dry: slightly sweet
  • Demi-sec: off-dry, sweet
  • Doux / Dolce: sweet

Watch out: "Extra dry" is sweeter than "Brut", even if the name suggests the opposite.

Storage

Sparkling wines are usually best drunk within 6–18 months of disgorging, also because homes rarely have the conditions to keep them long.

Crémant and Satèn

  • Crémant: the name for quality French sparkling wines (and other European ones) made with the Classic Method outside Champagne, with precise rules: hand harvest, gentle pressing, and the name of the area on the label. Originally it meant wines with gentler bubbles.
  • Satèn: a style of Franciacorta, only from white grapes and with less pressure, so with softer bubbles. The name recalls silk and satin.

Bubbles with the whole meal

In Italy most sparkling wine is opened between Christmas and New Year, but bubbles are great for the whole meal:

  • acidity and bubbles "clean" the mouth and prepare it for the next bite;
  • they don't cover dishes, they lift them.

Pairings: raw fish, shellfish, seafood, risotto, fried and grilled fish; cured meats like prosciutto crudo and culatello; a Rosé with lamb or rabbit; cheeses like Parmigiano or camembert; a Demi-sec with some desserts.

Sweet, dried-grape and fortified wines

5 min read

Fortified wines

Their colors go from straw to brown, with rich aromas (caramel, honey, almond, spice, dried figs and apricots, candied fruit) and bold but velvety flavors.

They're made by adding alcohol (or brandy, concentrated or cooked must) to a base wine. That's why they have a lot of alcohol (about 15–22%) and often a lot of sugar, though dry versions exist. The most famous are Marsala, Port, Sherry and Madeira.

Ice wines

The bunches stay on the vine until January and are picked frozen (below -7 °C). The water inside the berries is ice, so only a very thick juice is pressed out, full of sugar, acidity and flavor.

They're called Icewine (Canada, especially Ontario) and Eiswein (Germany, Austria). The best grapes are riesling and gewürztraminer; in Italy they're very rare. They're golden and smell of honey, baked apple, exotic fruit and sweet spice. They're very sweet but fresh, thanks to their acidity.

Late harvest

The grapes stay on the vine a few extra weeks. They get sweeter and slightly shriveled, while acidity drops a little. The juice can make a sweet wine (stopping fermentation) or a dry but more alcoholic, structured wine (letting it finish).

Aromatic grapes give the best results: riesling, gewürztraminer, sauvignon, moscato, malvasia. Famous "Vendemmia tardiva" wines are made in Alto Adige, Trentino, Veneto, Alsace, Germany and Austria. They're great with desserts, foie gras and washed-rind cheeses.

A special case is Friuli's Picolit: by nature its bunches have very few, very concentrated berries. It's a prized dessert wine, golden, with aromas of raisins, honey and dried apricot.

Drying the grapes (passiti)

The grapes are left to dry after picking: they lose water and concentrate sugars and aromas.

  • on the vine, rarely (for example Aleatico di Gradoli, in Lazio);
  • in the sun, in hot areas (Moscato di Pantelleria, Greco di Bianco in Calabria);
  • indoors, on racks, in crates or hung on wires, in well-aired rooms, checking that no harmful molds appear (for example Torcolato di Breganze);
  • today often also with artificial ventilation, which shortens the time a lot.

The yield is very low: 100 kg of grapes give only 25–30 liters of wine. The grapes are pressed between December and February; for Tuscan Vin Santo and Trentino's Vino Santo they sometimes wait until Holy Week.

Some great Italian passiti: Erbaluce Passito and Loazzolo (Piedmont), Moscato giallo and rosa and Gewürztraminer (Alto Adige), Recioto di Soave (Veneto), Albana Passito (Romagna), Sagrantino Passito (Umbria), Malvasia delle Lipari and Moscato di Pantelleria (Sicily). Some famous dry reds are also made from dried grapes, like Amarone della Valpolicella and Sforzato di Valtellina.

On the nose and palate: raisins, dried fig, exotic and canned fruit, dried apricot, honey, jam, vanilla; a sweet, velvety taste.

Pairings: blue cheeses (like gorgonzola) or very aged cheeses, even with honey and jams; dry, spiced pastries; on their own as a meditation wine after dinner.

Botrytis cinerea (noble rot)

It's usually a mold that ruins grapes, but with the right climate (humid mornings and sunny afternoons) it becomes "noble": it pierces the skin, lets the water evaporate and concentrates sugars and aromas. It gives the wine more softness (more glycerol) and an unmistakable aroma.

The bunches look ugly, shriveled and gray-brown, but they make extraordinary sweet wines. The harvest is often done in several passes, picking only the bunches that are ready each time.

The great botrytized wines:

  • Sauternes (France, near Bordeaux): from sémillon with a little sauvignon. The most famous is Château d'Yquem. Rich and soft, with about 14% alcohol;
  • Trockenbeerenauslese (Germany and Austria): very sweet but low in alcohol (7–9%). Fresher from riesling, softer from gewürztraminer;
  • Tokaji Aszú (Hungary): from the furmint grape. A paste of botrytized grapes is added to a base wine, measured in puttonyos (the harvest baskets, from 3 to 6): the more puttonyos, the sweeter the wine. The rarest is Eszencia, very dense and very sweet. Aromas of honey, candied fruit, raisins, dried figs, vanilla.

Italy has no typical area for botrytized wines, but a few are made in the center-north.

Marsala

It's Italy's most famous fortified wine, made in the province of Trapani (Sicily).

The history: its roots go back to the Phoenicians, but Marsala as we know it was born around 1770 thanks to the English merchant John Woodhouse. To ship the wine to England without it spoiling, he added alcohol. It was a huge success: even Admiral Nelson loved it. Other Englishmen followed and finally the Italian Florio family, who exported it worldwide. In the 20th century its image was ruined by poor products like "egg Marsala"; today many producers are relaunching it.

The grapes: white (grillo, catarratto, inzolia, damaschino) for Marsala Oro and Ambra; red (nero d'Avola, nerello mascalese, pignatello) for the rare Rubino.

How it's made: alcohol is added to the base wine and, depending on the type, cooked must (which gives an amber color and caramel notes) or concentrated must. Vergine has none. Then the wine rests in barrels not filled to the top, so air makes it evolve: the typical "oxidative" note that would be a fault in other wines is its character here.

By color: Oro, Ambra, Rubino. By sweetness: dry, semi-dry, sweet.

By aging (from youngest):

  • Fine: at least 1 year
  • Superiore: at least 2 years
  • Superiore Riserva: at least 4 years
  • Vergine / Soleras: at least 5 years, always dry
  • Vergine Stravecchio / Riserva: at least 10 years

On the nose: wood, vanilla, caramel, toasted almond, licorice, candied citrus, honey, sweet spice.

How to serve it: cool, around 12–14 °C, in a small tulip glass.

Pairings: dry Vergine and Superiore as an aperitif, with nuts and snacks, or with fish dishes and savory sauces; Superiore with foie gras or blue cheeses (gorgonzola, roquefort, stilton); the sweet version with rich desserts and chocolate.

Italy's wine

2 min read

Land and climate

Italy sits at the heart of the ideal band for vines: from north to south there's a great variety of climates, from alpine cold to almost tropical heat, but the Mediterranean climate prevails. That's why there isn't a single region without vineyards.

  • The Alps protect from the northern cold; the Apennines run the length of the peninsula.
  • The sea, around almost the whole country, softens the climate. Lakes (Garda, Maggiore, Como, Iseo, Trasimeno) and rivers keep the air cooler and more humid in dry periods.
  • Over 40% of the land is hilly, and it's on hills that the best grapes grow: sun, wind, good drainage, less mold, cool nights.
  • Soils are very varied. Clay, limestone, marl and tuff (Langhe, Alto Adige, Tuscan hills, Campania) give colorful, aromatic, long-lived wines. Sandy soils along some coasts give more delicate wines to drink young.
  • The vintage (how the weather went that year) is still decisive: there are memorable years and difficult ones.

A few numbers

Italy makes about 18% of the world's wine and is among the top producers in the world. More than a third of Italian wine is exported. In recent years the average level has risen a lot: today, next to the few famous wines, there's a base of excellent quality. There are a great many denominations: over 70 DOCG and more than 300 DOC.

Grapes of the regions (a selection)

Every region has its signature varieties, next to the international ones (chardonnay, pinot, sauvignon, merlot, cabernet). Some examples:

  • Valle d'Aosta: petit rouge, prié blanc
  • Piedmont: nebbiolo, barbera, dolcetto, moscato bianco, cortese, arneis, grignolino, brachetto, freisa
  • Lombardy: nebbiolo (called chiavennasca in Valtellina), croatina, uva rara
  • Trentino-Alto Adige: teroldego, lagrein, marzemino, schiava, nosiola, gewürztraminer, müller-thurgau
  • Veneto: corvina, rondinella and molinara (Valpolicella), garganega (Soave), glera (Prosecco), raboso
  • Friuli-Venezia Giulia: ribolla gialla, friulano, malvasia istriana, refosco, picolit
  • Liguria: vermentino, pigato
  • Emilia-Romagna: lambruschi, albana, pignoletto, sangiovese
  • Tuscany: sangiovese, canaiolo, vernaccia di San Gimignano, trebbiano
  • Marche: verdicchio, montepulciano
  • Umbria: sagrantino, grechetto
  • Lazio: cesanese, malvasia
  • Abruzzo: montepulciano, trebbiano abruzzese
  • Molise: tintilia
  • Campania: aglianico, fiano, greco, falanghina, piedirosso, coda di volpe
  • Puglia: primitivo, negroamaro, nero di Troia
  • Basilicata: aglianico
  • Calabria: gaglioppo, greco bianco
  • Sicily: nero d'Avola, nerello mascalese, frappato, grillo, catarratto, zibibbo (moscato d'Alessandria)
  • Sardinia: cannonau, carignano, monica, vermentino, malvasia, nuragus

The other great fortified wines

3 min read

Sherry (Spain)

It's born around Jerez de la Frontera, in Andalusia, on a white chalky soil called albariza. The main grape is palomino; for sweet versions pedro ximénez and moscatel are used.

It starts as a dry white wine to which alcohol is added. Then the wine rests in oak barrels not filled to the top. For Fino, a veil of yeast called flor forms on the surface and protects it from air: the wine stays pale and delicate. Without flor, or when the flor breaks, air ages the wine "oxidatively" and it turns dark, with aromas of dried fruit.

The solera system. Barrels are stacked in several rows. Ready wine is taken from the lowest row (the solera), which is refilled with wine from the row above, which in turn is topped up with even younger wine, and so on. This way the lowest barrel always holds a little of the oldest wine, sometimes from a century ago.

The main styles

  • Fino: pale, dry and fresh, smelling of yeast and almond. To drink young.
  • Manzanilla: an even more elegant and savory Fino, made by the sea (Sanlúcar de Barrameda).
  • Amontillado: the flor developed only partly; amber, dry, more structured, smelling of dried fruit.
  • Oloroso: no flor; dark (mahogany), robust and soft, tasting of walnut.
  • Palo Cortado: rare, halfway between Fino and Oloroso.
  • Cream and Pale Cream: sweetened versions.
  • Pedro Ximénez: the sweetest. Almost black, dense, tasting of caramel, dried figs, dates, chocolate. Perfect with cocoa desserts and dried fruit, and one of the few wines that stand up to chocolate.

Port (Portugal)

The most famous fortified wine in the world. It's made in the Douro valley, in northern Portugal, from many different grapes, mostly red (the finest is touriga nacional).

How it's made: the must starts fermenting, and while it still has a lot of sugar brandy is added. Fermentation stops and the wine stays sweet and strong. Then it ages in traditional barrels (pipes), historically in the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia.

The main styles

  • Ruby: the youngest, bright ruby, fruity.
  • Tawny: long aging in barrel. It turns garnet-orange, soft and complex. The label may show its average age: 10, 20, 30, over 40 years.
  • Vintage: the most prestigious, made only in the best years (shown on the label). It spends little time in barrel and then ages in bottle for 20–30 years.
  • Late Bottled Vintage (LBV): from a single year, but it stays in barrel longer (4–6 years).
  • White Port: more delicate and often dry, to drink chilled as an aperitif.

Pairings: white Port as an aperitif; sweet Port with biscuits and dry pastries; more mature reds with aged and blue cheeses; a great Tawny on its own, after dinner.

Madeira (Portugal)

It's born on the island of Madeira, from vines on volcanic terraces facing the sea. Its secret is heating: the wine is kept for months at 40–50 °C, which gives its typical caramel, bittersweet, smoky taste. Like Port, it's fortified with alcohol.

It's named after the grape, from driest to sweetest:

  • Sercial: amber, sharp, dry and delicate. Perfect as an aperitif.
  • Verdelho: more structured and a little sweet, with smoky and honey notes.
  • Bual: sweeter, brown, with an intense, almost "burnt" scent. For after dinner or with rich desserts.
  • Malmsey (malvasia): the rarest and sweetest, aromatic, with notes of caramel and honey.

There are also Vintage Madeiras, from a single grape and a single year, aged in barrel for at least 20 years.

Denominations: DOP, IGP and the wine pyramid

3 min read

DOP and IGP

  • DOP (Protected Designation of Origin): the name of an area especially suited to wine. It guarantees that the wine comes from that area and is made following precise rules, written in a document called the disciplinare. The wine's character is closely tied to the land and to human work.
  • IGP (Protected Geographical Indication): a broader category. It says the wine has a link with a geographical area (usually larger), with less strict rules.

In Italy these categories correspond to the traditional abbreviations:

  • DOCG (Controlled and Guaranteed Designation of Origin) and DOC (Controlled Designation of Origin) correspond to DOP;
  • IGT (Typical Geographical Indication) corresponds to IGP.

On the label you can find the Italian abbreviation, the European one or both. In Alto Adige and Valle d'Aosta, because they're bilingual, you may also find names in German or French.

The wine pyramid (from the base to the top)

  1. Wines without denomination (once "table wines"): generic wines or wines named after the grape, with few rules.
  2. IGT / IGP: a large production area, lighter rules. It can name the grape. Many excellent wines are IGT, often because the producer wants freedom of choice.
  3. DOC: a precise area and rules set by the disciplinare.
  4. DOCG: even stricter rules and an extra check before bottling. Smaller areas (sub-zones) can be named too, such as a village, a hamlet or a single vineyard.

The higher you go, the smaller the area and the stricter the rules. Today, though, all denomination wines must be of quality anyway, so the pyramid mostly shows how tight the link with the land is.

In Italy about a third of wine is DOP, a third IGP and a third has no denomination.

The disciplinare

It's the "rulebook" of each denomination. Among other things it sets:

  • the production area;
  • the allowed grapes and their percentages;
  • how many grapes can be grown per hectare (maximum yields);
  • the minimum alcohol and the features the wine must have;
  • how to grow the vineyard (training systems, pruning);
  • sometimes also the minimum aging time, the obligation to bottle in the area, the type of bottle and closure.

How a wine becomes DOC or DOCG. One step at a time: to become DOC a wine must have been IGT for some years, and to become DOCG it must have been DOC for at least 10 years and be especially prized and well known. Each step means stricter rules. Before going on sale, DOC and DOCG wines are analyzed and tasted by a commission that certifies their quality.

Consorzi di Tutela bring together the producers of a denomination: they protect it from imitations and promote it.

Words on the label: Classico, Riserva, Superiore, Novello, Passito, Vigna

  • Classico: the wine comes from the oldest, historic zone of the denomination (for example Chianti Classico). For sparkling wines "Storico" is used.
  • Riserva: the wine has aged longer than usual. At least 2 years for reds, 1 year for whites, 3 years for Classic Method sparkling wines (1 for tank-method ones).
  • Superiore: higher quality. Fewer grapes per hectare and a little more alcohol than the "basic" wine of the same denomination.
  • Novello: a very young wine, made partly by carbonic maceration. It's sold from November 6 of the harvest year and must be bottled by December 31. The vintage is mandatory on the label.
  • Passito: wine made from dried grapes (naturally or in special rooms).
  • Vigna + name: the wine comes from a single precise vineyard, vinified separately.

For DOC and DOCG wines (except sparkling, semi-sparkling and fortified wines) the vintage on the label is mandatory.

The label

2 min read

The label is the wine's ID card: by law it says what's in the bottle, but it's also the first tool to attract buyers. Some were designed by great artists such as Chagall, Picasso, Matisse and Miró.

A bit of history

  • Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans already marked their amphorae.
  • In the Middle Ages small tags (of bone, ivory, metal) with the wine's name were hung on the amphorae.
  • The first paper labels appeared in Champagne shortly before 1750 (the first handwritten ones were Moët & Chandon's). From 1798, with lithographic printing, they spread all over Europe.
  • The first back label was Italian, from the early 1800s: on a bottle of Nebbiolo it showed the year of harvest, of bottling and how the wine was made.
  • In the 1940s–50s labels became real advertising images. Today the trend is toward simple, minimal labels.

Today's labels are often self-adhesive and no longer come off with warm water, as people once did to collect them.

What the law says

The label protects buyers (from fraud and wrong choices) and lets the producer tell the story of the wine. Some information is mandatory and some optional. The higher the level of the wine, the more numerous and precise the information.

The main information must be in the same field of vision, readable without turning the bottle.

Mandatory information

  • Product category: wine, sparkling wine, semi-sparkling wine, fortified wine… (it can be left out if there's a denomination).
  • Denomination: DOCG, DOC, IGT (or DOP/IGP), for wines that have one.
  • Alcohol in % vol (with a small tolerance from the real value).
  • Origin (for example "Product of Italy").
  • Bottler (name and address) and any importer.
  • Quantity (for example 750 ml).
  • Allergens: "Contains sulfites" is always mandatory; if used, others too, like albumin (egg) or casein (milk).
  • Production lot.
  • For sparkling wines: the sweetness level (brut, extra dry, demi-sec…).
  • For DOC and DOCG: the vintage (if at least 85% of the grapes are from that year).

Optional information

  • The vintage, for other wines (again with the 85% rule).
  • The grape: a single one can be named only if it's at least 85% of the grapes; if two or more are named, they must cover 100%.
  • How sweet it is, for still wines (from driest to sweetest): secco, abboccato, amabile, dolce.
  • Terms like Superiore, Novello, Riserva.
  • The European DOP and IGP logos.
  • How the wine was made: "barrel fermented", "aged in barrique", or for sparkling wines "Metodo Classico", "bottle fermented", "crémant".
  • A smaller area (village, hamlet, locality), if at least 85% of the grapes come from there.
  • Words like castello, abbazia, rocca, only if the wine is really made in that place.
  • The names of other operators in the chain (producer, distributor).

Everything written on the label, even if optional, must be true and must not confuse the consumer.

Serving temperatures

2 min read

Temperature changes a lot how a wine tastes. In general: the lighter, fresher or more sparkling the wine, the colder it should be served; the redder, more structured and tannic, the less cold.

Dry sparkling wines
4–6 °C
Sweet sparkling and semi-sparkling wines
6–8 °C
Young whites and rosés
8–10 °C
Structured and mature whites, white passiti and fortified wines
10–12 °C
Structured rosés, light low-tannin reds
12–14 °C
Medium-bodied reds
14–16 °C
Important and mature reds, red passiti and fortified wines
16–18 °C

Practical tips for home

  • To chill a white or a sparkling wine quickly, use an ice bucket with water and ice (about two thirds water and one third ice): it works better than ice alone.
  • A cooler sleeve (the insulated holder) doesn't chill wine, it keeps it cool.
  • Reds shouldn't be served at the "room temperature" of a warm home: they're better a little cool too.

Serving wine

2 min read

Serving wine takes attention and simplicity: no overly ceremonial gestures, which make people uneasy. The basic rules apply at home too.

From the cellar to the table

  • Carry the bottle gently, especially an old red, so as not to stir up the deposit at the bottom.
  • Whites and rosés: in an ice bucket with water and ice or in a cooler sleeve, to keep them cool. Dry the bottle before pouring.
  • To open it you need a good corkscrew (the sommelier's "two-step" one is the most practical) and a napkin.
  • After opening, it's worth smelling the cork and tasting a sip: if the wine has a fault (like cork taint) you notice right away.

Decanting a wine

Why decant

  1. To remove the deposit: old, important reds form a natural sediment at the bottom, which isn't a fault but shouldn't end up in the glass.
  2. To let the wine breathe: a wine closed in a bottle for years needs oxygen to open up all its aromas.

How to do it, simply

  1. Stand the bottle upright for a few hours beforehand, so the deposit settles at the bottom.
  2. Open it gently, without shaking it.
  3. Pour the wine into the carafe (the decanter) slowly and steadily, watching the bottle's neck. Sommeliers once used a candle under the bottle's shoulder to see well; at home a lamp or a flashlight is enough.
  4. Stop when the deposit reaches the neck: the little cloudy wine left stays in the bottle.

Just to aerate: if the wine has no deposit but is "closed" (for example an important white or a young red), a simple pour into a carafe is enough, with no special care. A small trick: letting the wine breathe in a carafe also helps light unpleasant smells disappear, like the pungent one of sulfites.

Wine glossary

B

Barrique

A small oak barrel of about 225 litres. The wine changes faster and takes on more aromas from the wood.

Botrytis cinerea

A mould that usually ruins grapes. In special conditions it becomes “noble rot” and gives great sweet wines.

D

Dosage

A touch of wine and sugar added at the end of the Classic Method. It decides how dry or sweet the sparkling wine will be.

G

Grafting

Joining a European vine onto American roots that resist phylloxera. It’s how most vines are planted today.

M

Malolactic fermentation

A second fermentation, done by useful bacteria, that softens the wine. Typical of reds.

P

Perlage

The trail of bubbles rising in a glass of sparkling wine.

Phylloxera

A small insect from America that attacks the roots. In the 1800s it destroyed about 85% of Europe’s vineyards.

R

Rootstock

The part of the vine with the roots, usually American, onto which the European vine is grafted.

S

Sulphites

Added to protect wine from air and unwanted microbes. That’s why labels say “contains sulphites”.

T

Tannins

Substances from grape skins and seeds that dry your mouth. Rough when young, softer after ageing in wood.

V

Veraison

In July and August the berries change colour and start to ripen.

No word found. Try another spelling.

Porcini mushroom risotto with Barolo

4 chapters · 12 min

Narrated by Chef Marco Sella · Text in every chapter

0:483:12

“I always use the Barolo I’d drink at the table. Never cook with a wine you wouldn’t want in your glass.”

Chef Marco Sella

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. A risotto is not rice with a sauce: it’s rice that slowly drinks its broth. I toast the Carnaroli dry until it’s too hot to touch, then add the broth one ladle at a time, for about eighteen minutes. The porcini go in a separate pan, fast and hot, so they stay firm and keep their scent of wood. They meet the rice only at the end.

  2. Barolo is Nebbiolo from the Langhe, and by law it waits at least three years before it leaves the cellar. Young, it is all tannin and acidity; with time it opens to rose, tar and dried cherry. For this dish I choose one with a few years on it: the tannins have softened and the wine has learned to listen.

  3. Porcini taste of forest floor; an aged Barolo smells of leaves, earth and truffle. Similar flavours call each other. Then the contrast does the rest: the butter and Parmigiano round off the tannins, and the wine’s acidity cleans the palate, so every spoonful tastes like the first.

  4. Open the bottle an hour before, or decant it. Serve it at 16 to 18 degrees, in a large glass where Nebbiolo has room to breathe. Pour it while the risotto rests for two minutes off the heat: that’s when the butter goes in and the first sip is ready for the first bite.

The pairing in one line

Earth meets earth

Porcini’s earthy umami softens Barolo’s tannins, while the wine’s acidity cuts through the butter and Parmigiano.

Ingredients

  • Carnaroli rice320 g
  • Fresh porcini400 g
  • Vegetable broth1.2 l
  • Shallot1
  • Barolo1 glass
  • Butter60 g
  • Parmigiano Reggiano 24 months70 g
  • Garlic1 clove
  • Parsleya handful
  • Extra virgin olive oil, salt, pepper

Method

  1. 1Clean the porcini with a brush and a damp cloth, then slice them. Keep the broth simmering.
  2. 2Sauté the porcini in a hot pan with oil and the garlic clove for 3–4 minutes. Season, add the parsley and set aside.
  3. 3Soften the chopped shallot in a little butter, add the rice and toast it for 2 minutes, stirring.
  4. 4Pour in the glass of Barolo and let it evaporate, then add the broth one ladle at a time for about 16 minutes.
  5. 5Stir in half the porcini, cook 2 more minutes, then take it off the heat.
  6. 6Beat in the cold butter and the Parmigiano, cover and rest for 2 minutes. Serve with the remaining porcini on top.

The pairing

What Vinly users chose for this recipe, and why it works.

The classic: the earthy notes of an aged Barolo meet the porcini, and butter and Parmigiano soften its tannins.

12%

Barbaresco DOCG

Red · Elegant · Floral

Nebbiolo too, a little lighter and more perfumed: a good choice if the Barolo you have is very young.

6%

Red · Fresh · Fruity

The everyday version: less structure, the same rose and cherry. It works when the risotto is lighter on butter.

Behind the pairing

The sommelier’s notes: why it works, the technique and the history.

The wine in the pan leaves its acidity and aromas in the rice. With the same bottle at the table, dish and glass speak the same language.

Yes: 40 g, soaked in warm water for 20 minutes. Filter the water and add it to the broth for more flavour.

Decant it two hours before, or pick a Barbaresco: its tannins are gentler at the same age.

Paccheri al sugo di baccalà e olive

4 chapters · 3 min

SLTold by Chef Serena Letta

Chapter 1 · A fish that has travelled

Narrated by Chef Serena Letta · Text in every chapter

0:000:40

“Salt cod should be treated like fresh fish: low heat and plenty of patience.”

Chef Serena Letta

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. Baccalà comes from Northern Europe packed in salt, and I soak it for three days, changing the water twice a day. In the pan I let it flake slowly into the tomato, never stirring hard.

  2. Sardinian Vermentino grows on granite soils swept by the mistral. It has citrus, Mediterranean herbs and a salty finish that recalls a winter beach.

  3. Taggiasca olives bring a bitter, fatty note. The wine’s acidity cleans it up and the citrus makes it brighter, without covering the fish.

  4. I serve the Vermentino at ten degrees. Colder, it loses the herbal scent, which is exactly what you want next to the olives.

The pairing in one line

Salt calls for salt

The Vermentino’s savoriness matches the baccalà, and its freshness lightens the sauce.

Ingredients

  • Paccheri320 g
  • Desalted baccalà400 g
  • Cherry tomatoes200 g
  • Taggiasca olives80 g
  • Garlic2 cloves
  • Extra virgin olive oil, parsley, saltto taste

Method

  1. 1Rinse the desalted baccalà and cut it into irregular pieces.
  2. 2Heat the oil in a pan, add the crushed garlic and let it brown. Add the halved cherry tomatoes and the olives.
  3. 3Cook the sauce for 10 minutes over medium heat. Add the baccalà, cover and cook for 15 minutes over low heat.
  4. 4Boil the paccheri al dente in plenty of salted water.
  5. 5Drain the paccheri and toss them in the sauce. Serve with plenty of fresh parsley.

The pairing

What Vinly users chose for this recipe, and why it works.

70%

Vermentino di Sardegna

Savory · Citrus · Fresh

The Vermentino’s lively acidity balances the intense saltiness of the baccalà. Citrus notes and sea-breeze minerality lift the Taggiasca olives without covering the fish. A pairing by territory: Sardinia and the Mediterranean.

25%

Greco di Tufo DOCG

Structured · Mineral · Persistent

Fuller-bodied than Vermentino, it stands up better to the richness of the desalted baccalà. Volcanic minerality and bitter-almond notes play surprisingly well with the Taggiasca olives.

5%

Etna Rosso DOC

Light · Savory · Elegant tannins

Etna’s Nerello Mascalese is a light red with soft tannins and high acidity, almost a structured white. The tomato and olive sauce is rich enough to carry an elegant red: it’s the structure of the sauce, not the protein, that decides the wine.

Behind the pairing

The sommelier’s notes: why it works, the technique and the history.

Stewing with tomato and olives creates a savory, acidic, slightly bitter sauce. Baccalà is a rich fish with intense saltiness: it needs a wine with good acidity to balance the salt, and citrus notes to lift the olives.

The baccalà is cooked in a tomato sauce with garlic and Taggiasca olives. Stewing adds savoriness and richness to the dish, so the wine needs marked acidity.

Sardinia and baccalà met centuries ago on the Mediterranean trade routes. Basque fishermen carried dried cod all over Europe, and the island adopted it with enthusiasm. Vermentino grows on granite soils brushed by the sea breeze: it tastes of the sea before it even meets the fish.

Spaghetti alle vongole in bianco

4 chapters · 3 min

MFTold by Chef Mario Falchi

Chapter 1 · The secret is the water

Narrated by Chef Mario Falchi · Text in every chapter

0:000:40

“Clams should open in the pan, not cook: thirty seconds too long and they turn to rubber.”

Chef Mario Falchi

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. I purge the clams for two hours in salted water. Their filtered juice is the real sauce: with the starch from the spaghetti it becomes a cream with no butter.

  2. Verdicchio comes from the hills near Jesi. It has almond, white flowers and a sharp acidity that lets it age well for years.

  3. Clams are sweet and salty at once. Verdicchio’s almond finish recalls the golden garlic, and its savoriness holds up next to the sea.

  4. Parsley goes in raw, at the last second. I pour the wine into a wide glass, so the almond scent comes before the sip.

The pairing in one line

The sea in the glass

Verdicchio’s minerality echoes the clams and its acidity keeps the pasta lively.

Ingredients

  • Spaghetti400 g
  • Carpet-shell clams (vongole veraci)500 g
  • Garlic3 cloves
  • Fresh parsleyplenty
  • Dry white wine150 ml
  • Extra virgin olive oilplenty
  • Chili pepper (optional), saltto taste

Method

  1. 1Purge the clams in salted water for 2 hours.
  2. 2In a large pan, fry the garlic, add the clams, pour in the white wine and cook over high heat until they open.
  3. 3Strain the cooking liquid. Cook the spaghetti very al dente and finish them in the pan, adding the strained liquid.
  4. 4The dish should be creamy, not dry. Finish with a shower of chopped parsley.

The pairing

What Vinly users chose for this recipe, and why it works.

Crisp · Mineral · Marine

Marked acidity and sea-like minerality, perfect for clams in bianco. The Classico Superiore version has more structure to stand up to the concentrated sauce.

35%

Fiano di Avellino

Structured · Hazelnut · Floral

From Campania, structured, with notes of hazelnut and wild flowers. Without tomato, the dish can carry a more important white.

20%

Vermentino di Gallura DOCG

Mineral · Salty · Structured

Gallura’s minerality with clams in bianco: more structured than the basic Sardinian version. Its intense saltiness brings out the sea in the dish.

Behind the pairing

The sommelier’s notes: why it works, the technique and the history.

Same principle as linguine, but in bianco, without tomato: the taste of the clams is purer and more marine. The cooking liquid with white wine is the sauce. It needs a white with sea-like minerality and lively acidity.

The clams open fast over high heat; finishing the pasta in the pan makes it creamy and concentrates the flavors.

Carpet-shell clams have lived on the sandy Mediterranean seabed for millennia. The in bianco version is the oldest: tomatoes only arrived in the 16th century. Neapolitan fishermen ate their clams on the boat, with bread. Verdicchio comes from the Marche, the Adriatic region par excellence, where the hills run down to the sea.

Bucatini all’amatriciana

4 chapters · 3 min

LBTold by Chef Lucia Benvenuti

Chapter 1 · Six ingredients, no more

Narrated by Chef Lucia Benvenuti · Text in every chapter

0:000:40

“Guanciale must stay soft inside and crisp outside: it shouldn’t dry out like pancetta.”

Chef Lucia Benvenuti

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. Guanciale, pecorino, tomato, chili, white wine and pasta. In Amatrice there’s no onion and no garlic: all the flavor has to come from the guanciale.

  2. Cesanese del Piglio grows in the hills south of Rome. It’s a medium-bodied red with cherry, pepper and tannins that don’t dry the mouth.

  3. The chili and the pepper in the pecorino find a similar spice in the Cesanese. The wine’s fruit rounds off the tomato’s acidity.

  4. The hole holds the sauce and the pasta stays al dente longer. I serve the wine at sixteen degrees, slightly cool.

The pairing in one line

Fat and fruit

Cesanese has red fruit and gentle tannins: it cuts the guanciale without fighting the tomato.

Ingredients

  • Bucatini400 g
  • Guanciale from Amatrice150 g
  • Peeled San Marzano tomatoes400 g
  • Pecorino (black rind)120 g
  • Dry white winehalf a glass
  • Fresh chili pepper1
  • Ground black pepper, saltto taste

Method

  1. 1Cut the guanciale into strips.
  2. 2Brown it in a pan without oil over medium heat, until crisp but not dry.
  3. 3Deglaze with the wine. Add the chili, then the tomatoes crushed by hand.
  4. 4Cook for 20 minutes.
  5. 5Cook the bucatini very al dente and finish them in the sauce. Toss with pecorino to taste.

The pairing

What Vinly users chose for this recipe, and why it works.

50%

Cesanese del Piglio DOCG

Medium body · Soft tannins · Spicy

Lazio’s red with Lazio’s most famous dish. Cesanese has medium body, soft tannins and a light spiciness that talks to the guanciale and the chili.

30%

Montepulciano d’Abruzzo

Robust · Warm · Ripe fruit

A robust, warm red with ripe fruit. It handles the saltiness of the pecorino and the richness of the guanciale. Abruzzo borders Lazio.

20%

Cerasuolo d’Abruzzo

Rosé · Structured · Red fruit

Abruzzo’s rosé, with unexpected structure: it cuts the fat of the guanciale while its red fruit lifts the tomato. Whoever expects only a red is surprised.

Behind the pairing

The sommelier’s notes: why it works, the technique and the history.

Guanciale is fatty and savory. Tomato is acidic. Pecorino is intensely salty and sharp. Chili adds heat. It needs a red with enough acidity for the tomato and enough body for the guanciale.

The guanciale must keep a soft heart with a crisp outside: it must not dry out like pancetta.

Amatriciana was born in Amatrice, in the mountains of Lazio near Abruzzo, as “gricia”: pasta with guanciale and pecorino, no tomato. Tomatoes arrived from the New World in the 16th century and changed the dish. The 2016 earthquake destroyed Amatrice, and Italian restaurants all over the world held solidarity dinners to rebuild it.

Pappardelle al ragù di cinghiale

4 chapters · 3 min

SLTold by Chef Serena Letta

Chapter 1 · Hours on the stove

Narrated by Chef Serena Letta · Text in every chapter

0:000:40

“Wild boar needs a whole night in the marinade: red wine makes it tender and takes away the gamey edge.”

Chef Serena Letta

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. I brown the marinated meat and let it cook for three hours with bay leaf, juniper and a glass of wine. Wide pappardelle catch the thick sauce.

  2. Morellino di Scansano is Sangiovese from the Maremma. The warmer climate gives it riper fruit and softer tannins than Chianti.

  3. The juniper in the ragù and the wine’s Mediterranean scrub notes recognise each other. Morellino’s tannins stand up to the meat.

  4. Boar ragù rested overnight tastes better. I open the bottle half an hour ahead, so the fruit can open up.

The pairing in one line

Woods and Maremma

Morellino brings ripe fruit and a balsamic note that suits the long, spiced ragù.

Ingredients

  • Fresh pappardelle400 g
  • Wild boar (shoulder or leg)600 g
  • Onion, carrot, celery1, 1, 2
  • Tuscan red wine300 ml
  • Peeled tomatoes150 ml
  • Garlic3 cloves
  • Extra virgin olive oil, black pepper, saltto taste

Method

  1. 1Marinate the boar in the wine with vegetables and spices for 24 hours.
  2. 2Drain it and brown the meat in olive oil.
  3. 3Add the vegetable soffritto, the strained marinade and the tomatoes.
  4. 4Cook covered over low heat for 2–3 hours, until the meat falls apart.
  5. 5Shred the meat roughly into the sauce. Cook the pappardelle al dente and toss them in the ragù.

The pairing

What Vinly users chose for this recipe, and why it works.

60%

Ripe fruit · Soft tannins · Balsamic

Sangiovese from the Tuscan Maremma, the same land where the boar is hunted. Present but soft tannins, ripe fruit, balsamic notes. A pairing by territory.

35%

Brunello di Montalcino

Powerful · Aged · Complex

The power of Brunello with game: a Tuscan luxury pairing. Aged Sangiovese stands up to the complexity of the marinated boar.

5%

Very tannic · Powerful · Intense

Italy’s most tannic wine with the most flavorful meat of the Tuscan hunt: a pairing of extreme power. Umbria meets Tuscany.

Behind the pairing

The sommelier’s notes: why it works, the technique and the history.

Wild boar is gamey, flavorful and slightly iron-like. The red-wine marinade and juniper add balsamic notes, and the long cooking concentrates the sauce. It needs a Tuscan red whose tannins bind with the game.

The marinade tames the gamey edge and tenderizes the meat. Slow cooking breaks down the fibers.

Wild boar has lived in the Tuscan forests since before written history: the Etruscans hunted it on the hills of Volterra and Populonia. In the Maremma the hunt is still a social ritual: hunters meet at dawn, come back at noon and cook the ragù together. Morellino di Scansano was born in the same wild Maremma.

Sogliola alla mugnaia

Narrated by Chef Mario Falchi · Text in every chapter

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. I dust the sole with flour and cook it whole in foaming butter. When the butter turns hazelnut-brown, I add lemon and parsley.

  2. Meursault is a village in the Côte de Beaune. Aged in oak, it smells of hazelnut, butter and wet stone.

  3. Brown butter and the oak in the wine speak the same language. The lemon in the dish finds its echo in the Meursault’s acidity.

Butter with butter

Meursault has the same roundness as brown butter and an acidity that cleans the palate.

Ingredients

  • Butter150 g
  • 00 flourto taste
  • Lemons2
  • Chopped parsleyto taste
  • Salt and pepperto taste

Method

  1. 1Flour the sole and shake off the excess.
  2. 2Heat half the butter in a pan until foaming. Cook the sole for 3 minutes per side.
  3. 3Take the sole out. In the same pan, melt the remaining butter until it turns hazelnut brown.
  4. 4Add the lemon juice (it will sizzle hard) and pour the meunière butter over the sole.
  5. 5Garnish with parsley.

Method

Chef Lucia Benvenuti

The story in 4 chapters

Listen or read, at your own pace.

  1. Scoglio has no fixed recipe: it depends on what the fisherman brings. Mussels, clams, prawns and squid, with split cherry tomatoes and a splash of white wine.

  2. In the Sannio Falanghina grows on clay hills inland in Campania. It has citrus, peach and a salinity that makes it perfect with fish.

  3. Each shellfish tastes different. Falanghina holds them together with its acidity, and the citrus notes brighten the tomato.

  4. Mussels are eaten with your hands and the empty shell becomes a spoon. The wine is cold, on the table in an ice bucket.

The pairing in one line

The white of the Sannio

Ingredients

  • Linguine320 g
  • Mussels and clams800 g
  • Prawns8
  • Squid200 g
  • Cherry tomatoes250 g
  • Garlic, parsley, white wineto taste

Method

  1. 1Open mussels and clams in a covered pan with garlic and a splash of wine. Strain the liquid.
  2. 2Sauté the squid rings and prawns briefly, then add the halved cherry tomatoes.
  3. 3Cook the linguine very al dente and finish them in the pan with the shellfish liquid.
  4. 4Add mussels and clams back, toss and finish with parsley.
